subtitle: Minnesota's European American heritage is many particular cultures. Learn that history, see how a majority's habits can become the default rule in institutions, and use fair process to check whether those defaults block access.
scope: For staff across DHS. This course covers documented European American history in Minnesota, how mainstream habits become institutional defaults, and practical ways to review those defaults under existing civil rights duties. It uses public sources and original practice cases. It does not assess any person, infer anyone's heritage from appearance, or make a finding about a current DHS process. Native American and Tribal-specific matters are referred to DHS Tribal and Urban Indian Relations and the person or area responsible. Participation in this learning is voluntary.
introTranscript: Minnesota's European American heritage includes German, Norwegian, Irish, Swedish, Finnish, Slovene and many other histories. Over time, some of the majority's habits became the default rules of our workplaces and services. This course respects that heritage, keeps the documented history, and shows how to check whether a default helps everyone or quietly blocks someone.

lessons.title: Many European American cultures, not one
lessons.summary: Describe the range of European American heritage in Minnesota using public data and history.
lessons.objective: Describe the range of European American heritage in Minnesota using public data and history.
objectives: Describe the range of European American heritage in Minnesota using public data and history.
Separate a particular heritage from a broad label such as "Scandinavian" or "European."
Choose wording that describes a heritage accurately without turning it into a profile.
takeaways: Minnesota's European American heritage is many particular cultures, languages, faiths and regional histories.
A broad label can hide real differences in when, why and how families arrived.
A heritage describes a connection, not a person's character, politics or beliefs.
lessons.statement: European American heritage in Minnesota is many particular stories, not one.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: Many European American cultures, not one
intro.body:
In the 2024 American Community Survey, Minnesotans most often reported German ancestry, about 1.6 million people. Norwegian, Irish, English, Swedish and Polish ancestry followed. Finnish, Italian, Czech, Dutch, Danish and Scottish ancestry also appear in large numbers. A person can report two ancestries, so the totals overlap.

These are different histories. Norwegian lodges such as the Daughters of Norway, founded in Minneapolis in 1897, gave working women a place to speak their own language and support one another. In 1880, very poor families from Connemara in western Ireland arrived in western Minnesota too late to plant. Most later settled in a St. Paul neighborhood that came to be called Connemara Patch.

The Iron Range tells another story. Its population grew from fewer than 5,000 people in 1885 to more than 100,000 by 1920. Immigrants were more than half of the Range's people and about 85 percent of mine workers. After 1910, Finns were the largest group, followed by Slovenes, Croats, Italians and Swedes.

In the practice case, Nell drafts a team newsletter for a heritage month. The draft says "Scandinavian Minnesotans" share one set of values. It then lists Lutheran faith, reserved manners and lutefisk as traits of all European American staff. The question is not whether those traditions are real. They are. The question is whether one picture fits millions of people with different roots, faiths and family histories.

What is the best revision?
lessons.keyStatement: Describe a heritage as a particular connection, not as a profile everyone must fit.

flashcards.back: The places a person's family came from, as the person reports it. The American Community Survey lets a person report up to two.
Traditions, language, faith or history a person may feel connected to. How much it matters is the person's own account.
The way of doing things that a workplace or system treats as normal, often without saying so.

flashcards.front: The rule everyone is measured against
flashcards.back: A standard that sets what counts as ordinary, on time, prepared or polite.
A list of traits assigned to everyone in a group. Profiles replace asking with assuming.

items.title: The numbers show variety
items.body: Public ancestry data lists more than a dozen large European ancestry groups in Minnesota. People also write "European" or "Scandinavian" when they do not know or do not choose to name one country. A single label cannot carry all of that.

items.title: History shows different starting points
items.body: Families from Connemara arrived poor and unready for a Minnesota winter. Iron Range miners came from Finland, Slovenia, Croatia and Italy to do dangerous work. Swedish immigrants founded colleges and hospitals. These are different routes, and the differences matter for understanding the state.

items.title: A heritage is not a character trait
items.body: A Norwegian lodge, an Irish neighborhood or a Finnish hall describes a real community. It does not tell you what a coworker believes, eats or values today. Ask what a heritage means to a person only when it is relevant, and accept "nothing in particular" as an answer.

tabs.label: One label for everyone
tabs.body: The newsletter says all European American staff share reserved manners and Lutheran faith. That turns a real tradition into a rule about people. It also leaves out Catholic, Jewish, Orthodox and nonreligious families, and families who arrived last decade.

tabs.label: No heritage at all
tabs.body: Another draft says European Americans "do not really have a culture." That erases real languages, faiths and histories that many Minnesotans still value. It also makes the majority's habits look like nobody's habits, which hides them from review.

tabs.label: Particular and accurate
tabs.body: A revised draft names a few documented communities, cites the source for each and invites staff to share a tradition if they wish. It does not assign a trait to anyone. This keeps the history and respects the person.

check.question: Which statement about European American heritage in Minnesota is accurate?
check.correct: It includes many particular ancestries and histories, and none of them tells you an individual's beliefs or habits.
wrong: It is one Scandinavian culture that most Minnesotans share in the same way.
It is not really a culture, so it does not need to be described.
A person's ancestry tells you which traditions they practice today.
check.feedbackCorrect: Public data and history both show variety. A heritage is a connection, and how it matters to a person is their own account.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Census ancestry data shows German, Norwegian, Irish, English, Swedish, Polish and many other ancestries. The histories differ too. Treating them as one culture, or as no culture, loses that accuracy. Ancestry alone does not tell you what anyone practices today.

items.text: German is the most commonly reported ancestry in Minnesota in the 2024 American Community Survey.
Immigrants were about 85 percent of Iron Range mine workers in the early 1900s.
"Some staff connect with Norwegian, Irish or Finnish traditions; share one if you wish."
"Many Minnesotans of European descent have roots in very different places and faiths."
"European American staff are reserved and Lutheran."
"People of European descent have no culture of their own."

lessons.next: Next: How a majority's habits became the default rule

scenario.context: Nell's newsletter draft describes all European American staff as reserved, Lutheran and Scandinavian.
options: Name a few documented communities with sources and invite staff to share a tradition if they choose.
Keep the draft, since those traditions are common in Minnesota.
Remove European American heritage from the newsletter because it is the majority.
responses: This keeps real history and leaves each person free to describe their own connection. No one is assigned a trait.
Common traditions are real, but the draft applies them to every person. That is a profile, and it leaves many families out.
Leaving the majority out makes its habits look like nobody's habits. Accurate, sourced history serves readers better.

lessons.transfer: Think of a label at work that groups many people as if they were one, or use Nell's newsletter. How would you reword it so it stays accurate?

move.control: You can describe a heritage accurately and leave each person free to define their own connection.
move.failure: A broad label becomes a profile, or the majority's culture is treated as invisible.
move.next: Think of a label at work that groups many people as if they were one, or use Nell's newsletter. How would you reword it so it stays accurate?

lessons.title: How a majority's habits became the default rule
lessons.summary: Explain how the habits of a majority can become the standard rule in an institution.
lessons.objective: Explain how the habits of a majority can become the standard rule in an institution.
objectives: Explain how the habits of a majority can become the standard rule in an institution.
Describe documented Minnesota history where rules drew a line by race.
Separate an honest account of history from blame directed at individuals today.
takeaways: Many early European immigrants faced pressure to give up their language and customs.
Housing rules in Minnesota once drew a line by race, and families of European descent ended up on the open side of it.
Over time, a majority's habits can become the rule everyone else is measured against.
lessons.statement: A habit becomes a default when it is built into the rules and stops being questioned.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: How a majority's habits became the default rule
intro.body:
Many immigrant groups on this list were once outsiders. The Minnesota Historical Society describes unequal treatment of newer Iron Range immigrants and the community institutions they built to support one another. Lodges such as the Daughters of Norway gave members a place to speak their native language.

Over generations, many of these families moved into the mainstream. Rules helped decide who could make that move. Racial covenants were clauses written into property deeds. They barred people who were not white from buying or living in a home. The University of Minnesota's Mapping Prejudice project has documented thousands of them in Minneapolis and Hennepin County.

Because these deeds drew the line by race, families of European descent, including recent immigrants, could buy homes that Black families could not. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis connects covenants, redlining and federal mortgage practices to Minnesota's homeownership gap. In 2021 it reported that the gap between white and Black households ranked among the largest in the nation.

This history explains how one group's habits and advantages became the ordinary standard. It is not a claim about anyone's character or effort. Nell's grandparents may have worked very hard. Rules also shaped which doors were open to them. Both can be true. The practice question is what the rule did, and whether a similar rule still shapes access today.

inThisLesson: Explain how the habits of a majority can become the standard rule in an institution.
Describe documented Minnesota history where rules drew a line by race.
Separate an honest account of history from blame directed at individuals today.
What is the most useful response?
lessons.keyStatement: Ask what a rule did, not what kind of person benefited from it.

items.title: Outsiders became insiders
items.body: Finnish, Slovene, Italian and Irish newcomers once faced suspicion and hard conditions. Over generations many joined the mainstream. Their customs, holidays and ways of working became part of what Minnesota institutions treat as normal.

items.title: Rules drew lines
items.body: Racial covenants were written into deeds and enforced by courts and lenders. Mapping Prejudice documents how they shaped Minneapolis neighborhoods. A rule that names race is easy to see. Its effects can last long after the words are gone.

items.title: History is not a verdict on a person
items.body: Knowing that a rule favored some families does not say anything about one person's effort. It does help explain why starting points differ. That understanding is useful when you design a process today.

tabs.label: Denying the history
tabs.body: A coworker says covenants are old news and cannot matter now. The Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis documents a homeownership gap that still follows those patterns. Denying documented history makes current gaps harder to understand.

tabs.label: Blaming a person
tabs.body: Another coworker says anyone of European descent should feel guilty. That turns a fact about rules into a judgment about individuals. It does not help anyone fix a current process.

tabs.label: Tracing what the rule did
tabs.body: A third response asks what the rule allowed, who it shut out and what effects remain. This keeps the facts and points to action: check whether today's rules produce unequal results.

check.question: What does the history of racial covenants in Minnesota show?
check.correct: Rules in deeds barred people who were not white from many homes, and those rules shaped who could build wealth through homeownership.
wrong: Every family of European descent had an easy life.
Covenants had no effects that anyone can measure today.
Immigrant families from Europe never faced hard conditions.
check.feedbackCorrect: Mapping Prejudice and the Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis document both the rules and their lasting effects on homeownership. The history is about rules, not individual character.
check.feedbackIncorrect: The documented history shows rules that drew a line by race and a homeownership gap that followed. It does not mean every European American family had an easy life. Many immigrants faced real hardship. Both facts belong in an accurate account.

items.text: Racial covenants barred people who were not white from buying or living in many Minneapolis homes.
Immigrants were more than half of the Iron Range population by the early 1900s.
Rules can open doors for one group while closing them for another.
Effort and an easier route can both be part of the same family story.
This history means every person of European descent should feel guilty.
Since European immigrants also struggled, the covenants did not matter.

lessons.next: Next: Find the default in an ordinary process

scenario.context: In a team discussion, a coworker says, "My family came here with nothing, so none of this housing history applies to me."
scenario.prompt: What is the most useful response?
options: Tell the coworker the history proves they had an unfair advantage.
Acknowledge the family's hardship and note that rules also shaped which neighborhoods were open to which families.
Drop the topic so no one feels uncomfortable.
responses: This turns a documented pattern into a judgment about one person. It is likely to end the conversation rather than build understanding.
This respects the family's story and keeps the documented history. Both can be true, and the team can then look at today's rules.
Dropping it leaves the history unexamined. A calm, sourced account helps the team understand current gaps.

lessons.transfer: Choose a rule in a program you know, or use the covenant example. What did the rule allow, and whom did it leave out?

move.control: You can keep documented history and respect individual effort at the same time.
move.failure: History is denied, or it is turned into blame directed at individuals.
move.next: Choose a rule in a program you know, or use the covenant example. What did the rule allow, and whom did it leave out?

lessons.title: Find the default in an ordinary process
lessons.summary: Identify mainstream defaults built into ordinary work processes.
lessons.objective: Identify mainstream defaults built into ordinary work processes.
objectives: Identify mainstream defaults built into ordinary work processes.
Trace a process step by step to see who it serves easily and who it does not.
Connect a default to existing duties under Title VI and the Americans with Disabilities Act.
takeaways: Defaults hide in schedules, forms, examples, names and expected manners.
A default is not wrong because it is common; it needs review when it blocks access.
Tracing a process step by step shows where a default creates a barrier.
lessons.statement: A default is easiest to see when you walk through the process as someone it was not built for.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: Find the default in an ordinary process
intro.body:
A mainstream default is the way of doing things a workplace treats as normal. Examples include business hours, English-only forms, a name field with one first name and one last name, and a holiday calendar. Others are quieter: expecting eye contact, small talk or a quick answer as signs of good faith.

Many of these defaults came from the habits of the majority that built Minnesota's institutions. That does not make them wrong. A shared schedule helps people coordinate. The question is whether a default stops someone from getting a service or a fair chance at a job.

Civil rights law already asks this question. Title VI of the Civil Rights Act bars discrimination by race, color or national origin in federally funded programs, and federal guidance applies it to language access. The Americans with Disabilities Act requires effective communication with people who have disabilities. The DHS Equity Policy asks staff to consider who is affected by their daily work.

In the practice case, Nell's team handles a callback process. Staff call each applicant back once, between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m., in English. Missed calls close the request. Nell walks through it as three applicants: one who works a day shift, one who speaks Somali at home, and one who is Deaf. Each meets the same rule. Each has a different chance of getting through it.

inThisLesson: Identify mainstream defaults built into ordinary work processes.
Trace a process step by step to see who it serves easily and who it does not.
Connect a default to existing duties under Title VI and the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Which change should Nell propose?
lessons.keyStatement: Walk through the process as several different people, then decide what to change.

items.title: What the default assumes
items.body: One daytime call in English assumes the person is free during the day, hears well on the phone and reads and speaks English. Those assumptions fit many people. They leave others with no realistic way to answer.

items.title: Where the law already speaks
items.body: Title VI guidance asks programs to provide language access. The Americans with Disabilities Act requires effective communication, such as relay services or written options. These duties apply to everyone the program serves.

items.title: What a fair fix looks like
items.body: Offer a second attempt at another time, a text or mail option, interpreter access and relay. Apply the same options to every applicant. Then check whether closed requests drop.

tabs.label: Keep the rule because it is equal
tabs.body: Everyone gets one call, so the process looks fair. But the same rule lands differently on people with different schedules, languages and disabilities. Equal steps can still produce unequal access.

tabs.label: Make an exception by group
tabs.body: A staff member suggests extra calls only for applicants from certain backgrounds. That treats people differently by a protected trait. It also misses applicants who need a different option for other reasons.

tabs.label: Change the process for everyone
tabs.body: Offer the same set of options to every applicant: a second time slot, written contact, interpreters and relay. This fixes the barrier without sorting people by background.

check.question: What is the best way to review a default like a single daytime callback?
check.correct: Trace the process as several different applicants, find where it fails, and offer the same improved options to everyone.
wrong: Keep it, because one call for everyone is equal treatment.
Offer extra calls only to applicants from certain racial or ethnic groups.
Wait until someone files a complaint before changing anything.
check.feedbackCorrect: Tracing the steps shows where the default blocks access. Offering the same options to all applicants addresses the barrier and treats everyone the same way.
check.feedbackIncorrect: An equal rule can still block people because of schedule, language or disability. Fixing that by group would treat people differently by a protected trait. Waiting for complaints leaves the barrier in place. The better path is to trace the process and improve it for everyone.

items.text: One phone call, during the workday, in English only.
A form with one box for a first name and one for a last name.
Offer every applicant a second time slot and a written option.
Provide interpreters and relay services to anyone who needs them.
Give extra callbacks only to applicants of one race.
Close requests faster to keep the queue short, without checking who is dropped.

lessons.next: Next: Ask what a habit means before judging it

scenario.context: Nell's team closes a request after one missed daytime call in English. Many closed requests come from applicants who work day shifts or need an interpreter.
options: Keep the current process because it treats everyone the same.
Add extra callbacks only for applicants from immigrant communities.
Offer every applicant a second attempt at another time, a written option, interpreters and relay, then track closed requests.
responses: The steps are the same, but the results are not. The pattern of closed requests shows a barrier worth fixing.
This sorts people by background, which civil rights law does not allow. It also misses others who need a different option.
This fixes the barrier for everyone, meets language access and effective communication duties, and measures whether it worked.

lessons.transfer: Pick one process you touch, or use Nell's callback process. Walk through it as three different people. Where does it get harder?

move.control: You can find a default by tracing a process and fix it with options open to everyone.
move.failure: A default is kept because it looks equal, or it is patched with group-only exceptions.
move.next: Pick one process you touch, or use Nell's callback process. Walk through it as three different people. Where does it get harder?

lessons.title: Ask what a habit means before judging it
lessons.summary: Recognize that habits like directness, pace and silence carry learned meanings.
lessons.objective: Recognize that habits like directness, pace and silence carry learned meanings.
objectives: Recognize that habits like directness, pace and silence carry learned meanings.
Ask a relevant question instead of reading a habit as a sign of character.
Keep the work standard clear while allowing different ways of meeting it.
takeaways: The same behavior can mean care to one person and avoidance to another.
Asking what someone needs is more accurate than guessing their motives.
The standard stays the same; the route to it can vary.
lessons.statement: Ask what a habit means before you decide what it says about a person.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: Ask what a habit means before judging it
intro.body:
Everyone learns habits about honesty, pace and respect. Many people who grew up in the mainstream do not notice theirs, because those habits match the workplace. The Council of Europe describes intercultural skill as noticing that your own ways are learned, too, and asking about meanings instead of assuming them.

In the practice case, two coworkers on Nell's team work differently. Emil raises a problem early, while the work is still rough. In his family's repair shop, naming a problem early was how you let others help. Nell first reads this as poor preparation.

Ada prefers time to think before discussing a sensitive case. In her family, a considered answer showed respect for the listener. Nell first reads her pause as avoidance. Neither habit is tied to an ancestry group. Both are particular to these two people.

Once Nell asks, the picture changes. Emil's early question is a request for help. Ada's pause is preparation. The work standard stays the same: the case must be reviewed accurately and on time. Nell can invite Emil's early questions and give Ada a short window to prepare. Both meet the same deadline.

inThisLesson: Recognize that habits like directness, pace and silence carry learned meanings.
Ask a relevant question instead of reading a habit as a sign of character.
Keep the work standard clear while allowing different ways of meeting it.
What should Nell do first?
lessons.keyStatement: Keep the standard; ask about the route.

items.title: Your own habits are learned too
items.body: A quick answer, direct eye contact or a polished first draft may feel like plain good practice. They are habits someone taught you. Noticing that helps you avoid measuring everyone against your own style.

items.title: Ask a relevant question
items.body: "What would help you prepare for this?" is a work question. "Is that a cultural thing?" asks someone to explain their background. Ask about the work, not the person's identity.

items.title: Keep the standard visible
items.body: Allowing different routes does not mean lowering the bar. State the deadline and the quality expected. Then let people reach it in ways that work for them.

tabs.label: Judge the habit
tabs.body: Nell decides Emil is careless and Ada is evasive. Both judgments are guesses about character. They could shape assignments and reviews unfairly.

tabs.label: Assign it to a group
tabs.body: Nell decides Emil's directness and Ada's pause come from their ancestry. That turns two personal accounts into group rules. It also invites stereotypes about coworkers who share the same heritage.

tabs.label: Ask, then adjust the route
tabs.body: Nell asks each person what helps them do the work well. The deadline and quality bar stay the same. The route changes slightly. That is fair, accurate and easy to apply to anyone.

check.question: Ada asks for a day to think before discussing a sensitive case. What is the most accurate response?
check.correct: Ask what she needs to prepare, confirm the deadline, and give the same option to anyone who asks.
wrong: Treat the pause as avoidance and note it in her review.
Assume the pause reflects her ancestry and stop asking.
Remove the deadline so she never feels rushed.
check.feedbackCorrect: Asking replaces a guess with information. Keeping the deadline keeps the standard, and offering the option to anyone keeps treatment equal.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Reading the pause as avoidance is a guess about character. Linking it to ancestry is a stereotype. Removing the deadline changes the standard. The better path is to ask, keep the standard and offer the same option to everyone.

items.text: Ask, "What would help you prepare for this?"
Notice that your own sense of a "good" pace was learned.
State the deadline and quality expected for everyone.
Offer the same preparation window to any team member who asks.
Decide a coworker is careless because they raise problems early.
Assume a pause means the person disagrees but will not say so.

lessons.next: Next: Test a default against the people it serves

scenario.context: Emil raises a concern about a case while it is still rough. Nell's first thought is that Emil did not prepare.
options: Tell Emil to bring only finished work in the future.
Ask Emil what kind of help he is looking for, then decide.
Decide this is how people from Emil's background work and accept it.
responses: This applies Nell's own habit as the rule. It may stop useful early warnings.
Asking gives Nell real information. Emil may be asking for help in time to keep the work on schedule.
This assigns the habit to a group. Emil's account is his own, and others with the same heritage may work differently.

lessons.transfer: Name one work habit you treat as simply "good practice," or use Emil's or Ada's case. Where might someone have learned a different meaning for it?

move.control: You can ask about a habit's meaning and keep the work standard the same for everyone.
move.failure: A habit is read as character, or a personal account becomes a group rule.
move.next: Name one work habit you treat as simply "good practice," or use Emil's or Ada's case. Where might someone have learned a different meaning for it?

lessons.title: Test a default against the people it serves
lessons.summary: Test a resource or notice with the people who receive it before treating it as finished.
lessons.objective: Test a resource or notice with the people who receive it before treating it as finished.
objectives: Test a resource or notice with the people who receive it before treating it as finished.
Separate a familiar example from an actual program requirement.
Use the DHS Equity Policy and the Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions that need them.
takeaways: The people who receive a notice are the best test of whether it works.
A familiar example is not the same as a program rule.
Some issues carry a formal duty that learning cannot delay.
lessons.statement: Test the resource with the people who use it, and keep formal duties on their own track.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: Test a default against the people it serves
intro.body:
In a separate practice case, Nell's team reviews a welcome guide for a DHS program. Every example shows a married couple with two children in one home. Other households appear only as exceptions in a footnote. The program's actual rules accept many household types.

The guide is not wrong on purpose. It reflects the household the writers saw as ordinary. But readers in a three-generation home, a single parent or a shared household may think the program is not for them. That is the default at work.

Nell's team can test the guide. They can ask a few people who receive it to read it and say what they understood. They can check who received the old version and who applied. They can confirm the household definition with the person or area responsible for the program, so a friendlier example does not change a legal rule by accident. For a significant change, the DHS Equity Policy and the State of Minnesota Equity Analysis Toolkit offer structured questions.

A different situation calls for a different track. In the same week, a supervisor named Morgan hears an allegation of a race-related slur on the team. Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436 requires managers and supervisors to report protected-class allegations right away to Human Resources or the person the agency designates. Morgan reports it the same day. Learning about defaults never delays that duty.

inThisLesson: Test a resource or notice with the people who receive it before treating it as finished.
Separate a familiar example from an actual program requirement.
Use the DHS Equity Policy and the Equity Analysis Toolkit for decisions that need them.
Which plan handles both correctly?
lessons.keyStatement: Test with readers, confirm the rule, and report formal concerns without delay.

items.title: Test with the people who receive it
items.body: A short read-through with a few recipients shows what they understood and where they stopped. This is faster and more accurate than guessing. Offer the test in the languages and formats the program uses.

items.title: Confirm the actual rule
items.body: The person or area responsible for the program confirms what the household definition is. The guide should describe that rule clearly and show examples that match it.

items.title: Keep formal duties separate
items.body: A harassment allegation is not a learning exercise. Policy 1436 sets the reporting duty, and Human Resources or the designated person handles the process. The team can keep learning, but the report comes first.

tabs.label: Rewrite from instinct
tabs.body: The team replaces the examples with ones they like. They do not test the guide or confirm the rule. The new version may be friendlier but still miss readers, or it may misstate eligibility.

tabs.label: Test and confirm
tabs.body: The team asks a few recipients to read it, checks who applied after the old version, and confirms the rule. Then they revise and measure again. This is the approach the Equity Analysis Toolkit supports.

tabs.label: Mix the two tracks
tabs.body: Morgan decides to bring the slur allegation to the team's learning session instead of reporting it. That delays a required report. It also exposes the people involved.

check.question: Which step best tests whether the welcome guide works for the people it serves?
check.correct: Ask a few people who receive the guide to read it and say what they understood, then confirm the household rule with the program.
wrong: Ask the writers whether they think the guide is clear.
Change the examples and publish without checking the program rule.
Assume the guide works because no one has complained.
check.feedbackCorrect: Readers show what the guide communicates. Confirming the rule keeps the revision accurate. Together these make the change both fair and correct.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Writers already know what they meant, so they are not a good test. Publishing without checking the rule can create a new error. A lack of complaints does not show that readers understood. Test with recipients and confirm the rule.

items.text: Ask three recipients to read the guide and describe what it says.
Compare who received the old guide with who applied.
Check the household definition with the person or area responsible.
Make sure new examples match what the program actually accepts.
Report a protected-class allegation to Human Resources the same day.
Follow the agency's assigned procedure rather than handling it within the team.

scenario.context: Nell's team wants to revise the welcome guide. Separately, Morgan has heard an allegation of a race-related slur on the team.
options: Test the guide with recipients and confirm the rule; Morgan reports the allegation the same day under Policy 1436.
Revise the guide from instinct; Morgan raises the allegation at the next team learning session.
Pause the guide revision until the allegation is resolved, and hold the report until then.
responses: Each issue goes on its proper track. The guide improves through testing, and the formal duty is met right away.
The guide is not tested, and a required report is delayed. A learning session is not the place for an allegation.
The guide revision can continue. Holding the report delays a duty that Policy 1436 requires right away.

lessons.transfer: Pick one notice or resource you use, or use Nell's welcome guide. Who could you ask to read it, and what would you want to learn from them?

move.control: You can test a resource with its readers and keep formal duties on their own track.
move.failure: A resource is revised from instinct, or a formal duty is delayed by informal discussion.
move.next: Pick one notice or resource you use, or use Nell's welcome guide. Who could you ask to read it, and what would you want to learn from them?

lessons.summary: Explain that civil rights protections cover people of every race and national origin, including European Americans.

Recognize remarks about heritage, accent or ancestry that can cross into national origin harassment.
Plan a fair-process change, measure its results and revisit it.
takeaways: Title VII and the Minnesota Human Rights Act protect every employee from discrimination by race and national origin.
Jokes about any heritage or accent can become harassment.
Fair process means the same clear criteria for everyone, checked by results.
lessons.statement: Fair treatment applies to everyone, and fair processes are checked by their results.

image.caption: Colleagues listen to one another around a conference table with laptops and notes.

intro.heading: Fair treatment for everyone, including the majority
intro.body:
Civil rights law protects every person. Title VII of the Civil Rights Act and the Minnesota Human Rights Act bar employment discrimination because of race, national origin and other protected traits. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's national origin guidance covers ancestry, ethnicity and accent. That includes people of Norwegian, Irish, Polish or Finnish descent, and people from the Iron Range.

The commission's March 2025 technical assistance on workplace discrimination makes the same point. Training, groups and opportunities must be open to all employees. Decisions cannot be based on race or national origin, whatever group is involved.

In the practice case, a coworker keeps mocking another employee's Iron Range accent and uses an old ethnic slur about her Slovene family. The team laughs it off as harmless. It is not harmless. Repeated slurs about someone's ancestry can be national origin harassment. The supervisor addresses it and follows the reporting policy.

This course ends where it began: with fair process. Notice the default. Trace the process. Ask instead of assuming. Test with the people affected. Apply the same criteria to everyone. Then measure the results and revisit. These steps work for the majority and for everyone else.

lessons.keyStatement: Use the same fair process for everyone, then check whether it worked.

items.title: Protections cover everyone
items.body: Title VII and the Minnesota Human Rights Act protect employees of every race and national origin. A slur about an Irish, Finnish or Slovene heritage is a national origin issue, just as a slur about any other heritage would be.

items.title: Open to all
items.body: Learning sessions, mentoring and heritage events should be open to every employee. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's guidance warns against limiting them by race or national origin.

items.title: Measure and revisit
items.body: After a change, check the results. Did closed requests drop? Did more eligible households apply? Write down what you changed and why, and set a date to look again.

tabs.label: Treat it as a joke
tabs.body: The team says jokes about European heritage do not count. Civil rights law disagrees. Repeated slurs about anyone's ancestry can create a hostile workplace.

tabs.label: Sort opportunities by group
tabs.body: A manager proposes a mentoring program open only to certain racial groups. That treats people differently by race. A fair version is open to everyone and uses clear criteria.

tabs.label: Apply fair process and measure
tabs.body: The supervisor addresses the slur and reports it. The team keeps its callback and guide changes, opens them to all, and checks the results in three months.

check.question: A coworker repeatedly mocks a colleague's Iron Range accent and uses an old slur about her Slovene family. What is accurate?
check.correct: This can be national origin harassment, and the supervisor should address it and follow the reporting policy.
wrong: It is not a civil rights issue because the colleague is of European descent.
It is harmless as long as the colleague laughs along.
It should be handled only in an optional learning session.
check.feedbackCorrect: National origin protections cover every ancestry. Repeated slurs can create a hostile workplace, and supervisors have a reporting duty.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Civil rights protections apply to everyone, including people of European descent. A person may laugh along to avoid conflict. A learning session does not replace the reporting duty. Address it and report it.

items.text: An employee of Finnish descent is protected from national origin harassment.
An applicant of any race is protected from race discrimination in hiring.
Use the same written criteria for every candidate.
Check results three months after a change and adjust.
Open a mentoring program only to employees of certain races.
Ignore repeated jokes about a coworker's ancestry.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to notice defaults, trace processes, ask instead of assuming, and check results.

scenario.context: A manager wants to start a mentoring program. One proposal limits it to employees of certain races. Another opens it to everyone with clear criteria.
scenario.prompt: Which approach should the manager choose?
options: Limit the program to certain racial groups to correct past patterns.
Skip the program because any program might raise concerns.
Open the program to everyone, publish clear criteria, and check who applies and who is selected.
responses: This treats people differently by race. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission's guidance says opportunities must be open to all.
Mentoring can widen access. A fair design is better than no program.
This is open to all, uses visible criteria and measures results. If some employees are not learning about it, the manager can widen outreach to everyone.

lessons.transfer: Choose one change you could make within your role, or use the mentoring case. What criteria would you write down, and what result would you check in three months?

move.control: You can apply the same fair process to everyone and check whether it works.
move.failure: Protections are applied to some groups only, or a change is made and never measured.
move.next: Choose one change you could make within your role, or use the mentoring case. What criteria would you write down, and what result would you check in three months?

jobAid.subtitle: Respect particular heritage, notice the mainstream default, and use fair process to check it.
remember: European American heritage is many particular histories; a heritage is a connection, not a profile.
A default is not wrong because it is common. Review it when it blocks access to a service or a fair chance at work.
Fix barriers with options open to everyone. Never sort people by race or national origin.
Managers and supervisors report protected-class allegations right away under Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436.

sections.heading: Describe heritage accurately
items: Use public sources, such as American Community Survey ancestry data and the Minnesota Historical Society.
Name particular communities instead of one broad label.
Invite people to share a tradition if they wish; never assign one.
Keep documented history, including rules such as racial covenants, with a named source.

sections.heading: Find and test the default
items: Trace the process step by step as several different people.
Note what it assumes about schedule, language, disability, household and manners.
Ask a relevant work question instead of guessing what a habit means.
Test notices and resources with the people who receive them.
Confirm the actual rule with the person or area responsible before changing an example.

sections.heading: Apply fair process and check results
items: Write clear criteria and apply them to everyone.
Provide language access and effective communication to anyone who needs them.
Use the DHS Equity Policy and the Equity Analysis Toolkit for significant changes.
Write down what you changed and why, measure the result, and set a date to revisit.

sources.title: United States Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2024, table B04006 (People Reporting Ancestry), Minnesota, via Census Reporter
sources.note: Supports the most commonly reported European ancestries in Minnesota (German about 1.6 million, then Norwegian, Irish, English, Swedish and Polish). One-year estimates with margins of error; a person may report two ancestries.

sources.title: Minnesota Historical Society, MNopedia: Immigration to the Iron Range, 1880–1930
sources.note: Supports Iron Range population growth, the immigrant share of residents and mine workers, the largest immigrant groups after 1910, unequal treatment of newer immigrants and the community institutions they built.

sources.title: Minnesota Historical Society, MNopedia: Connemara Patch, St. Paul
sources.note: Supports the 1880 arrival of poor families from Connemara in western Minnesota and their later settlement in St. Paul.

sources.title: Minnesota Historical Society, MNopedia: Daughters of Norway
sources.note: Supports the 1897 Minneapolis founding of the Daughters of Norway and its role for Norwegian working women.

sources.title: Minnesota Historical Society, MNopedia: Swedish Immigration to Minnesota
sources.note: Supports the colleges, hospitals and social service institutions founded by Swedish immigrants.

sources.title: American Swedish Institute: Mission and values
sources.note: Background on a Minnesota institution devoted to Swedish and Swedish American heritage. An institution's mission does not describe any individual's identity or preferences.

sources.title: University of Minnesota Libraries, Mapping Prejudice
sources.note: Supports the definition of racial covenants and the project's documentation of covenants in Minneapolis and Hennepin County.

sources.title: Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis: Systemic racism haunts homeownership rates in Minnesota (2021)
sources.note: Quoted by its published title. Supports the history of covenants, redlining and federal mortgage practices, and the finding that Minnesota's homeownership gap ranked among the largest nationally as of the article's date.

sources.title: United States Department of Justice and federal partners: Limited English proficiency resources (lep.gov)
sources.note: Supports the application of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act to language access in federally funded programs.

sources.title: United States Department of Justice: Americans with Disabilities Act, effective communication
sources.note: Supports the duty to communicate effectively with people who have disabilities, including relay and written options.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: Enforcement Guidance on National Origin Discrimination
sources.note: Supports coverage of ancestry, ethnicity and accent under Title VII, and national origin harassment, for employees of every national origin.

sources.title: Equal Employment Opportunity Commission: What You Should Know About DEI-Related Discrimination at Work (March 2025)
sources.note: Quoted by its real title. Supports the point that Title VII protects all employees and that training, mentoring and other opportunities may not be limited by race or national origin.

sources.title: Minnesota Statutes, section 363A.08 (Minnesota Human Rights Act, unfair employment practices)
sources.note: Supports state protection from employment discrimination because of race, national origin and other protected traits.

sources.title: DHS Equity Policy
sources.note: Supports the expectation that staff consider who is affected by daily work and use formal analysis where it applies. This voluntary course does not complete a required analysis.

sources.title: State of Minnesota: Equity Analysis Toolkit, A Quick Guide
sources.note: Supports structured questions for reviewing who a significant change affects and how to measure results.

sources.title: Minnesota Management and Budget Policy 1436: Harassment and Discrimination Prohibited
sources.note: Supports the duty of managers and supervisors to report protected-class allegations right away and follow assigned agency procedures. This course makes no finding.

sources.title: Council of Europe: Developing intercultural competence through education
sources.note: Supports the idea that everyone's habits are learned and that intercultural skill means asking about meanings instead of assuming them. Informs the Emil and Ada practice case.
